issues.legal_issue: A suit brought by a deity through its manager against the person managing the temple is not subject to the sanction requirement for suits concerning public trusts.
material_facts: The suit was brought by the deity through its manager against the person in management of the temple.
The temple property was not property of a public religious or charitable trust.
The suit was not brought by relators.
issues.conclusion: The suit was maintainable without the written sanction of the Advocate-General.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not apply because the suit was brought by the deity against the person managing its property, rather than by relators, and the property was not that of a public religious or charitable trust.

predicates.deity_suit_against_temple_manager: A deity brought a civil suit through its manager against the person managing the temple.
predicates.temple_property_not_public_trust: The temple property was not property of a public religious or charitable trust.

issues.definition: When a deity sues the person managing its temple property and that property is not part of a public trust, the suit proceeds without public-trust sanction.

issues.legal_issue: A state that has made substantial donations to a temple has a sufficient interest to maintain a suit on the deity’s behalf to protect temple property.
material_facts: The suit was brought on the deity’s behalf to protect the temple and its property.
The state had made large donations from time to time for the maintenance of the temple.
It was not proved that the state’s ruler had established the temple or installed the deity.
issues.conclusion: The state had a substantial interest to maintain the suit on behalf of the deity to protect its property.
issues.legal_principle: The court held that substantial donations for maintenance of the temple gave the state a sufficient interest to maintain the protective suit, even though it was not proved to be the temple’s founder or installer of the deity.

predicates.deity_protection_suit: A state brought or supported a suit on a deity’s behalf to protect temple property.
predicates.state_made_substantial_temple_donations: A state made substantial donations from time to time for the maintenance of a temple.

issues.definition: When a state supports a suit to protect a deity’s property and has made substantial donations for maintaining the temple, it has sufficient interest to maintain the suit.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court has jurisdiction to frame a management scheme for a private temple and its property.
material_facts: The temple was a private religious endowment rather than a public trust.
The suit concerned protection and management of the temple and its property.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to frame a scheme for management of the temple and its property.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradywnna Kumar Mullick, 52 I.A. 245, which directed a scheme for regulating worship despite the absence of a public trust, and on Asha Bibi v. Nabissa Sahib and Shri Mahadeo Jew v. Balkrishna Vyas, which supported the maintainability of suits concerning management of private religious endowments.

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_temple_management: A civil suit concerned the protection or management of a temple and its property.
predicates.temple_is_private_endowment: The temple and its property formed a private religious endowment rather than a public trust.

issues.definition: When a civil suit concerns a temple that is a private religious endowment, the civil court may frame a scheme for its management.

issues.legal_issue: An incumbent who mismanages temple property, uses it for personal benefit, and asserts personal title to it is unfit to continue in temple management.
material_facts: The incumbent committed acts of mismanagement and misappropriation concerning the temple and its property.
The incumbent asserted personal title to temple property and converted property to personal use.
The incumbent had constructed residential buildings on the temple premises and used part of them to lodge pilgrims.
issues.conclusion: The incumbent was not fit to remain in possession as the temple’s priest or manager and was liable to be removed from the temple and its properties.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated mismanagement, misappropriation, conversion of endowment property to personal use, and assertion of personal title as conduct incompatible with continuing as priest or manager of the temple.

predicates.temple_management_case: A case concerned the management of a temple and its property.
predicates.incumbent_misappropriated_temple_propert: The person managing the temple misappropriated its property or converted it to personal use.
predicates.incumbent_asserted_personal_title: The person managing the temple claimed personal ownership of temple property.

issues.definition: In a temple-management case, a manager who misappropriates temple property and claims it as personal property is unfit to continue managing the temple.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may direct the lower court to frame a management scheme, appoint a manager, and take accounts to make an effective decree protecting a private temple endowment.
material_facts: The matter was an appeal from a decree concerning possession and management of a temple and its property.
The temple was in a different state from the state whose officials had pursued the suit, making it difficult for those officials to administer the temple and protect its property.
The incumbent had mismanaged and misappropriated temple property.
The court considered a scheme for management, protection of the property, and an accounting of the incumbent’s dealings necessary.
issues.conclusion: Exercising its power under Order 41 Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court directed the court of first instance to frame a management scheme, appoint a manager with authority to take possession and administer the property under the court’s directions, take accounts from the incumbent, determine and recover any amount due, and make appropriate orders concerning the incumbent’s constructions and private use of the property.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowered the appellate court to make an effective decree by directing the lower court to frame a scheme and provide for management, accounting, and protection of the private religious endowment; the scheme was to be consistent with applicable law concerning private religious endowments.

rule.if: appeal_from_temple_management_decree and remote_state_administration_is_difficult and temple_property_needs_protection and incumbent_mismanaged_temple_property

predicates.appeal_from_temple_management_decree: An appeal arose from a decree concerning management or possession of a temple and its property.
predicates.remote_state_administration_is_difficult: Officials pursuing the suit were based in a different state from the temple, making effective administration difficult.
predicates.temple_property_needs_protection: The temple property required protection from misappropriation or private use.
predicates.incumbent_mismanaged_temple_property: The incumbent managing the temple mismanaged or misappropriated its property.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a temple-management decree, administration from another state is difficult, and the property needs protection from an incumbent’s mismanagement, the appellate court may direct the lower court to arrange management and accounting.
